newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia's Proton to roll out one millionth car.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia's Proton to roll out one millionth car.

text.p: After 11 years of production, Malaysia's first national car maker Proton is set to roll out its one millionth unit on Monday.

The guest of honour at the at the ceremony at Proton's production plant in Shah Alam -- an industrial area just outside capital city Kuala Lumpur -- will be Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, the mastermind behind the car project.
Mahathir is also expected to unveil a new 1.8-litre coupe.
And though the road ahead may be slightly bumpy, analysts say the company is likely to motor along without too many breakdowns.

Already, Proton's acquisition of British sports car maker Lotus Group International Ltd in October for 51 million sterling has put it in good stead to develop its own engines and transmission systems.

"In the early years the emphasis was on production. They just wanted to produce as many cars as possible, and since it is a protected market, they did not worry too much about (developing) their own technology," said Choo Swee Kee, analyst at equities research house Vickers Ballas in Kuala Lumpur.

Proton (Perusahaan Otomobil Nasional Bhd) makes family saloon cars named Saga, Iswara, Wira and Perdana, and a three-door hatchback, Satria. In Europe, the Wira is called Persona and the Satria, the Persona Compact.
When the first Proton rolled off the production lines in 1985 in a venture with Japan's Mitsubishi Motors Corp, the company was at the vanguard of Mahathir's industrialisation programme.
As such the Malaysian government made sure that Proton was protected from competition from foreign car makers by slapping on a 300 percent import tariff.
But international trade agreements will bring down tariffs on foreign imported cars by 1998, forcing Proton to cut costs as one way to become more competitive.

"They are aiming to cut costs by 15 percent over the next five to six years. This year their costs will be cut by around three percent, but it gets harder to cut costs as you get nearer the bone," said Lim Kim See, automotive analyst at Omega Securities.
Another way to achieve greater economies of scale is by producing more cars. Proton plans to turn out 230,000 cars a year by end of 1997 from 180,000 currently.
The company has also been aggressively marketing the cars overseas, pitting them with more experienced Japanese and European car makers.
Proton has won success in markets including Europe due to its low prices and strong after-sales support service, analysts said.
"They are behind on quality control, technology and cost efficiency," said Lim at Omega.
The Lotus acquisition was widely seen as a strategic one for Proton to absorb new car-making technology.

As Proton rolls out its one millionth car, analysts are confident that this is just another milestone on the road to becoming a world-class car maker. The car is already exported to some 30 countries.
"Whatever happens, the government will never allow Proton to die," said Choo at Vickers Ballas.
